# Dhātu Saṁyutta (SN 14)

**ID:** SN 14  
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Dhātu Saṁyutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul2.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul2.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dhātusaṁyutta* is the fourteenth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated as the third chapter of the *Nidānavagga* [Bodhi 2003]. Bhikkhu Bodhi suggests it was intentionally arranged as a "junior partner" to the *Nidānasamyutta*, sharing a concern with the fundamental principles of Buddhist phenomenology and causality rather than literary ornamentation [Bodhi 2003]. The commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*) glosses the elements (*dhātu*) in this collection as having an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) characterized by voidness and the absence of a permanent living being (*nissattattha-suññatāttha*) [Bodhi 2003].

Although "element" in early Buddhism often designates the four material elements (earth, water, fire, and air), they occupy only a minor role here; the collection instead investigates disparate groups of phenomena, principally eighteen, six, and four elements [Bodhi 2005]. The primary analysis centers on the eighteen elements of sensory perception (the six faculties, six objects, and six corresponding consciousnesses) [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2005]. Other discourses apply the triad of gratification (*assāda*), danger (*ādīnava*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*) to the material elements (SN 14.31–33) [Bodhi 2005], or describe unique meditative schemes, such as the seven elements of light, beauty, and formless attainments in the *Sattadhātusutta* (SN 14.11) [Polak 2011]. The samyutta also examines how individuals come together according to matching dispositions; for instance, the *Caṅkamasutta* (SN 14.15) describes pupils congregating around teachers of corresponding inclinations, such as Ānanda's followers who cherish learning or Anuruddha's disciples who cultivate the divine eye [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Modern scholars note that these discourses on beings congregating by shared elements and dispositions prefigure later theories of spiritual "lineage" (*gotra*) in Abhidharma and Mahāyāna traditions [Nyanatusita 2013].

A corresponding *Dhātusaṁyutta* section exists in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99, especially in fascicles 17 and 21) [Watanabe 1983], and SN 14.15 has an additional parallel in the *Ekottarikāgama* (EA 49.3).

**Sources**

- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, Connected Discourses of the Buddha (2003) — Contextual placement in Nidānavagga, opening sutta on eighteen elements, and commentary's explanation of dhātu as empty of a self.
- [Bodhi 2005] Bhikkhu Bodhi, In the Buddha's Words (2005) — Analysis of the clusters of elements (eighteen, four, six) and application of the assāda-ādīnava-nissaraṇa formula.
- [Nyanatusita 2013] Bhikkhu Nyanatusita (ed.), The Bodhisattva Ideal (2013) — Prefigurations of gotra (spiritual lineage) theory in the Dhātusaṁyutta.
- [Nyanaponika et al. 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha (2003) — Citations of SN 14.15 regarding disciples gathering around Ānanda and Anuruddha by common inclination.
- [Polak 2011] Grzegorz Polak, Reexamining Jhāna (2011) — Discussion of the Sattadhātusutta (SN 14.11) and the scheme of seven meditative elements.
- [Watanabe 1983] Fumimaro Watanabe, Philosophy and its Development in the Nikāyas and Abhidhamma (1983) — Parallel categorization of khandha, āyatana, and dhātu in both the Pali Saṁyuttanikāya and the Chinese Samyuktāgama.
